prompt: The board wants instant payout live before the end of the quarter. In McConnell's three words, what is that date?
hint: Who wants it, and for what reason?

choices.text: An estimate
choices.why: An estimate is a prediction of how long the work takes; the board's date says nothing about the work.

choices.text: A commitment from the Payments team
choices.why: A commitment is a promise made by people who know both the estimate and the target; nobody in Payments has promised this.

choices.text: A target
choices.why: Right: a date the business wants for reasons of its own. It becomes a commitment when a team that knows the estimate agrees to it.

choices.text: A contingency on the plan
choices.why: A contingency is a planned reaction to a risk, which is a different idea from a date somebody wants.

prompt: A piece of work is estimated at O = 3, M = 5 and P = 13 weeks. What is its PERT mean, in weeks?
For the same piece of work (O = 3, M = 5, P = 13 weeks), what is the PERT standard deviation, in weeks? Two decimal places or one are both fine.
hint: A sixth of the whole range.

prompt: In Renata's table the sum of the most likely values is 12 weeks and the sum of the PERT means is 13.5. Where does the extra week and a half come from?
hint: Compare how far P and O each sit from M.

choices.text: A safety margin Renata added on top of the team's numbers
choices.why: Nobody added anything: the means come straight from the team's own three numbers.

choices.text: Each P sits further above M than each O sits below it
choices.why: Right: software work has more room to run late than early, so each mean lands above its most likely value.

choices.text: The formula weights the pessimistic value four times
choices.why: The weight of four goes to M, the most likely value; P and O count once each.

choices.text: Standard deviations were added to the most likely values
choices.why: The means use no standard deviation at all; the spread is a separate number.

prompt: By the lesson, what makes the cone of uncertainty narrow?
hint: A month of waiting leaves it as wide as it was.

choices.text: Time passing on the project
choices.why: Waiting without deciding leaves the range as wide as before; the calendar narrows nothing.

choices.text: A more senior person giving the estimate
choices.why: Seniority does not remove the unknowns; the people doing the work estimate it best.

choices.text: Smaller tickets
choices.why: Breaking work down helps estimate it, but pieces cut around an open question are still uncertain.

choices.text: Decisions that remove what was unknown
choices.why: Right: deciding what a payout does when the bank is down, for example, takes width out of the range.

prompt: At the stage of an initial idea, the actual effort lands between a quarter and ___ times the estimate.
hint: The widest end of the cone.

prompt: Who fills in the O, M and P numbers for the instant payout work, and why?
hint: Renata asked questions; she did not write numbers.

choices.text: The Payments engineers who will do the work
choices.why: Right: the people doing the work estimate it, and a team held to somebody else's number has a reason to miss it.

choices.text: Renata, because she sees the whole design across teams
choices.why: Her own estimates are for choosing between options; delivery estimates belong to the team.

choices.text: Helena, because she owns the date the board will see
choices.why: Helena owns the target. Mixing target and estimate is the confusion the section starts with.

choices.text: Sílvio's finance team, who price a team-week
choices.why: Finance turns weeks into reais afterwards; it does not know how long the code takes.

prompt: The bank's payout API goes down on a Friday evening, and drivers are waiting. In the register, what has R3 become?
hint: A risk is something that has not happened yet.

choices.text: A risk with a higher score than before
choices.why: Raising the score treats it as something that might happen; it already has.

choices.text: An issue, handled as ordinary work
choices.why: Right: a risk that happens leaves the register and is handled rather than assessed.

choices.text: A risk transferred to the bank
choices.why: Transfer is a response chosen in advance, such as a contract; it does not describe an event that happened.

choices.text: An accepted risk, to be closed
choices.why: Accepting is a decision made before the event, and closing the row would lose the work the outage needs.

prompt: A risk has a 15% chance of happening in a quarter and would cost R$ 240,000 if it did. What is its exposure per quarter, in reais?
hint: Probability times impact.

prompt: Match each response to the action Carreto took with it.
hint: Avoid changes the plan; transfer hands the consequence to somebody else.

pairs.right: pay only to the Pix key verified at registration
cap instant payouts for drivers with few deliveries
a provider that carries most of a bank outage
live with app store delays, with the screen shipped early

right_distractors: put the risk on the last slide of the proposal

prompt: In a register scored 1 to 5, a data-centre fire that would stop Carreto for a month scores 1 × 5, and a slow weekly report scores 5 × 1. What should Renata do with that?
hint: The product hides the shape.

choices.text: Treat them as equal, since both of them share a score of 5
choices.why: Equal scores are exactly the trap: one is a nuisance and the other is a question of survival.

choices.text: Drop the fire from the register, since its likelihood is the lowest
choices.why: Low likelihood is no reason to ignore an impact the company might not survive.

choices.text: Read the fire's impact alone: would Carreto survive it?
choices.why: Right: for each impact of 5, the lesson reads that column alone, whatever the likelihood.

choices.text: Switch to a scale of 1 to 10 for finer scores
choices.why: A finer scale keeps the same problem: a product of two ordered ratings still hides which axis is high.

prompt: In risk-storming, why does each person write risks on sticky notes alone before anybody talks?
hint: Think about who speaks first in a group.

choices.text: To save time in the meeting
choices.why: Writing alone takes ten minutes of the meeting; the reason is what it protects, not speed.

choices.text: So the notes stay anonymous, even to the architect running it
choices.why: The notes go on the diagram and the group discusses them openly afterwards.

choices.text: So the most senior voice does not decide what the rest noticed
choices.why: Right: once one person names the risks, the rest of the room repeats them instead of adding their own.

choices.text: Because each risk is scored by each person and then averaged
choices.why: Nothing is averaged; the notes are clustered on the diagram and talked through.

prompt: If the bank's sandbox misbehaves (R2), both the bank integration and the reconciliation testing run late. What does that do to the 1.89-week spread of the total?
hint: The arithmetic assumed the pieces vary independently.

choices.text: It stays the same, since the spread counts each row
choices.why: The rows are counted, but as if they moved independently; a shared cause breaks that.

choices.text: It shrinks, because one cause is easier to manage than two
choices.why: A shared cause makes the pieces run late together, which widens the total.

choices.text: It is too narrow: shared causes make the real spread wider than that
choices.why: Right: and the habit the lesson asks for is to write the shared unknown down as a risk.

choices.text: It should be replaced by the sum of the standard deviations
choices.why: Adding the deviations assumes every piece runs late together, which overstates it; the fix is naming the shared cause.

prompt: What turns accepting a risk into a decision rather than an oversight?
hint: R5, the app store.

choices.text: A score below 5
choices.why: A low score explains why acceptance is reasonable; it does not make it a decision.

choices.text: An owner and a contingency, written down
choices.why: Right: R5 is accepted on paper, owned by Diego, with the screen shipped a week early behind a flag.

choices.text: The product director's signature on the register
choices.why: Helena decides on options; a signature does not replace an owner who watches the row.

choices.text: Leaving it off the register to keep it short
choices.why: That is the oversight itself: a risk nobody wrote down was never accepted, only missed.

prompt: What is the output of a spike?
hint: The four parts of the discipline.

choices.text: A written answer to a written question
choices.why: Right: with a time box, and with its code thrown away or marked as a prototype.

choices.text: A first, rough version of the feature itself
choices.why: A spike that becomes the feature is the failure the time box exists to stop.

choices.text: A revised risk register for the project
choices.why: The answer may change the register, but the spike's product is the answer itself.

choices.text: A library the team adopts
choices.why: A spike may try a library; adopting one is a decision taken after the answer.

prompt: Of the four rows in Renata's table, why did the spike go to the proof-of-delivery checks?
hint: Width, and whether a few days could change it.

choices.text: It had the largest most likely value of the four rows
choices.why: Its M was 3 weeks, below the ledger's 4; size of the work is not what a spike targets.

choices.text: The widest range, from an answerable question
choices.why: Right: 1 to 9 weeks, because nobody knew what Tracking records at delivery; three days found out.

choices.text: Tracking had spare engineers free to work on it that week
choices.why: Availability helps run a spike; it is not why this row was chosen.

choices.text: Sílvio's finance team asked for it
choices.why: Sílvio cared about R1, the fraud risk; the spike was chosen from the estimate's widths.

prompt: Option X costs R$ 150,000 more to build than option Y and saves R$ 25,000 a month to run. After how many months has X paid back its extra cost?
hint: Extra cost divided by the monthly saving.

prompt: Why does Renata's page include option C, doing nothing?
hint: What did Helena ask about in the first place?

choices.text: It is the cheapest option, so it is the default choice
choices.why: It has a cost of its own, drivers leaving, so it is not the cheapest by default.

choices.text: Templates for decision pages require three options
choices.why: No template is involved; the option is there because of what it costs.

choices.text: To show the board that the architect really did consider the whole field
choices.why: That would be decoration; option C is on the page because it changes the decision.

choices.text: Its own cost is the baseline A and B are measured against
choices.why: Right: 90 to 270 drivers a quarter by Helena's estimate, and leaving it off makes A and B look like the sole choices.

prompt: Put the steps of Renata's work on instant payout in the order the lesson tells them.
hint: Estimate, then risks, then information, then the choice, then imagining failure.
items: The Payments team gives O, M and P for each piece
A risk-storming session on the container diagram
A spike on the widest row of the estimate
A page comparing A, B and doing nothing
Helena and Sílvio choose B with an exit door
trap: Running the pre-mortem before a plan is chosen turns it into an ordinary risk list; its force comes from questioning a plan people already believe in.

prompt: A pre-mortem opens with "It is six months from now and the project was a disaster; write down why" rather than "What could go wrong?". What does that wording buy?
hint: A fact to explain, or a forecast to defend?

choices.text: Failure becomes a fact to explain, not a forecast to defend
choices.why: Right: the group is explaining an outcome rather than attacking a plan, so people say what they had kept quiet.

choices.text: A longer list of risks than a normal planning meeting produces
choices.why: Length is not the point; Renata's session found two new items, both important.

choices.text: Precise probabilities for each failure
choices.why: The exercise produces reasons, not numbers; those are rated afterwards in the register.

choices.text: A way to cancel the plan before it starts
choices.why: The plan stays; what changes is the register and the estimate, as with R6 and the support screen.

prompt: Kátia Lemos asks Renata for a page on rewriting the matching engine before the board meets. Which belong on it, by this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ranges, risks with names, options, and whose decision it is.

choices.text: A range to plan against, with its assumptions beside it
choices.why: Yes: a number without its width hides the part the board needs.

choices.text: One delivery date, so the board has something firm
choices.why: A single date at this stage is a corridor number on a slide; it will be read as a commitment.

choices.text: Keeping today's engine as an option, with what that costs
choices.why: Yes: doing nothing is the baseline against which a rewrite is worth anything.

choices.text: The largest risks, each with an owner and a response
choices.why: Yes: a risk without an owner and a response is a bullet nobody rereads.

choices.text: Renata's choice of winner, so the board can approve it quickly
choices.why: The page makes the consequences explicit; choosing belongs to the people who own the product and the money.

prompt: At the stage of an initial idea, a team says a migration will take 10 weeks. By the cone, what is the upper end of the real range, in weeks?
hint: The widest end of the cone, times the estimate.

prompt: After launch, drivers call support about a late payout, and support has no screen showing where a payout is. Which of the lesson's techniques was built to find that before launch?
hint: One technique walks the diagram; the other looks at the whole plan meeting people.

choices.text: Risk-storming on the container diagram
choices.why: Risk-storming finds failures in the parts and the arrows; support is not a box on that diagram.

choices.text: A three-point estimate of the support work
choices.why: You can estimate the screen only once somebody has noticed it is needed.

choices.text: A spike on the payout provider
choices.why: A spike answers a technical question somebody already asked; nobody had asked about support.

choices.text: A pre-mortem on the chosen plan
choices.why: Right: it looks for failure where the system meets people, and in Renata's session it found exactly this.

prompt: Renata's spike could have confirmed the pessimistic 9 weeks instead of shrinking them. Would it still have been worth the six person-days?
hint: What does a spike buy?

choices.text: No, because the planning number would not have moved
choices.why: The range would have narrowed around a worse number, which is still information the plan needed.

choices.text: Yes: it buys an answer, and a bad answer makes the plan honest
choices.why: Right: Helena's commitment would have rested on the real number instead of a hope.

choices.text: Yes, because spikes shorten projects
choices.why: A spike shortens nothing by itself; this one happened to bring good news.

choices.text: No, because Tracking's engineer lost three days
choices.why: Three days against a range of 1 to 9 weeks is a cheap price for the answer either way.
